items.prompt: Every sound is made by something ___.
hints: Touch your throat gently while you hum.
Pluck a stretched rubber band and watch it closely.
The word means moving quickly backwards and forwards. It starts with the letter v.
items.explanation: Every sound is made by something vibrating, which means moving quickly backwards and forwards. The vibrations travel through the air to our ears.

items.prompt: Match each instrument to the part that vibrates to make its sound.
hints: Ask which part of each instrument you pluck, hit, blow into or shake.
In a wind instrument, it is the air that vibrates.
Start with the guitar. Think about what you pluck with your fingers.
items.explanation: Guitar strings, drum skins and metal gongs vibrate when they are plucked or struck. In a flute the air inside the tube vibrates, and an angklung's bamboo tubes vibrate when it is shaken.

items.prompt: Ari puts his ear on one end of a table. Beni gently taps the other end. Ari hears the tap clearly. What does this show?

options.text: Sound can only travel through air.
options.why: Ari's ear was pressed on the table, so the sound came through the wood.

options.text: Tables make their own sounds.
options.why: The table only carried the vibrations from Beni's tap.

options.text: Sound can travel through solids.
Sound can only travel through water.
options.why: Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases.

hints: Ari's ear is touching the table, not open to the air.
The tap makes the wood vibrate.
Ask what the vibrations travelled through to reach Ari's ear.
items.explanation: The tap makes the table vibrate, and the vibrations travel through the solid wood to Ari's ear. Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases.

items.prompt: How can you make a drum sound louder?

options.text: Hit it more gently.
options.why: Gentle taps make small vibrations and quieter sounds.

options.text: Tighten the skin.
options.why: Tightening the skin makes the pitch higher. It does not make the drum louder.

options.text: Put a cloth on the skin.
options.why: A cloth muffles the drum and makes it quieter.

options.text: Hit it harder, so the skin makes bigger vibrations.

hints: Loudness depends on the size of the vibrations.
Bigger vibrations carry more energy to your ears.
Think about what you do with the stick to make a big vibration.
items.explanation: Hitting the drum harder makes the skin vibrate with bigger movements, so the sound is louder. Changing how tight the skin is changes the pitch instead.

items.prompt: Sort these into higher pitch and lower pitch.
hints: Pitch means how high or low a note sounds.
Faster vibrations make higher notes. Short, thin or tight things vibrate faster.
Compare the two angklung tubes first.
items.explanation: Short, thin, tight or small things vibrate faster and make higher notes. Long, thick, loose or large things vibrate more slowly and make lower notes.

items.prompt: Nina has four identical bottles with different amounts of water. She blows across the top of each one. Which bottle makes the highest note?

options.text: the bottle with the least water
options.why: That bottle has the longest column of air, which vibrates slowly and gives a low note.

options.text: the bottle with the most water
the bottle that is half full
options.why: It has more air inside than the fullest bottle, so its note is lower.

options.text: all four bottles make the same note
options.why: The column of air is a different length in each bottle, so the notes are different.

hints: When you blow across a bottle, the air inside it vibrates.
A shorter column of air vibrates faster and makes a higher note.
Find the bottle with the smallest space of air above the water.
items.explanation: Blowing makes the air in the bottle vibrate. The bottle with the most water has the shortest column of air, which vibrates fastest and gives the highest note.

items.prompt: Choose all the materials that would help to muffle sound in a music room.

options.text: thick curtains
carpet
foam panels
glass windows
options.why: Hard, smooth glass reflects sound instead of soaking it up.

options.text: metal sheets
options.why: Hard metal reflects sound, so the room would echo more.

hints: Muffling means soaking up sound so less of it bounces around.
Soft materials with lots of tiny air gaps absorb sound well.
For each material, ask whether it is soft and squashy or hard and smooth.
items.explanation: Soft materials such as curtains, carpet and foam absorb sound, so they muffle it. Hard, smooth surfaces such as glass and metal reflect sound back into the room.

items.prompt: Many small bats hunt insects in the dark. How do they find the insects?

options.text: They make high sounds and listen for the echoes that bounce back.
They see light given out by every insect.
options.why: Most insects do not glow, so the bats use sound to find them.

options.text: They smell each insect from far away.
options.why: These bats find flying insects using echoes of their own calls.

options.text: They feel the insects with their wings.
options.why: The insects are too far away to touch until the bat catches them.

hints: An echo is a sound that bounces back off a surface.
These bats make calls that are too high for people to hear.
Think about what happens when a bat's call hits an insect in front of it.
items.explanation: Insect-eating bats make very high sounds that bounce off insects as echoes. By listening to the echoes, the bats can tell where the insects are, even in the dark.

items.prompt: Astronauts on a spacewalk use radios to talk to each other. Why can they not hear each other shout?

options.text: Space is too cold for sound to work.
options.why: Temperature is not the problem. Sound needs a material to travel through.

options.text: Sound travels too fast in space to hear.
options.why: Sound cannot travel through empty space at all.

options.text: Space is almost empty, so nothing carries the sound vibrations.
Shouting makes no vibrations in a spacesuit.
options.why: Their voices still vibrate, but nothing outside the suits passes the vibrations on.

hints: Sound travels as vibrations passed from particle to particle.
Think about what fills the space between two astronauts outside a spacecraft.
Ask what sound needs to travel through, and whether space has it.
items.explanation: Sound needs a material, such as air, water or a solid, to pass its vibrations along. Space is almost empty, so sound cannot travel through it, but radio signals can.

items.prompt: Nina has four identical glass bottles with different amounts of water. She taps each one with a metal spoon. Which bottle makes the highest note?

options.text: the bottle with the most water
options.why: When you tap, the glass and the water vibrate together. More water makes slower vibrations and a lower note.

options.text: all four bottles make the same note
options.why: Each bottle holds a different amount of water, so each one vibrates differently.

options.text: the bottle that is half full
options.why: It has more water than the emptiest bottle, so its note is lower.

options.text: the bottle with the least water

hints: Tapping makes the glass vibrate, together with the water inside it.
More water makes the vibrating bottle heavier, so it vibrates more slowly.
Compare this with blowing across the bottles, where the column of air vibrates.
items.explanation: When you tap a bottle, the glass and the water inside it vibrate. Less water means faster vibrations, so the bottle with the least water gives the highest note, the opposite of blowing.

items.prompt: Label the parts that carry a sound to a listener.

figure.alt: A drum on the left, a row of wavy lines in the middle that show the air shaking, and an ear on the right.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The sound starts at the drum.
The wavy lines show the air shaking.
items.explanation: The drum is the source. It makes the air vibrate, and the vibrations travel to the ear.

items.prompt: Dewi sprinkles rice on a drum and hits it. Label the diagram.

figure.alt: A drum with a thin skin on top and a stick coming down from the top left. Three grains of rice are bouncing on the drum skin.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The rice jumps because the skin shakes.
The skin is the thin top of the drum.
items.explanation: The stick hits the skin and makes it vibrate. The shaking skin makes the rice grains jump.

items.prompt: Dewi holds each ruler on the desk and twangs the end that sticks out. Tap the ruler that makes the highest sound.

figure.alt: A desk edge on the left. Four rulers lie across it, each with part sticking out over the edge. Row 1 sticks out far, row 2 sticks out a medium amount, row 3 sticks out the least and row 4 sticks out a lot.

hints: Pitch is how high or low a sound is.
A shorter part vibrates faster.
Faster vibrations make a higher pitch. Find the shortest part sticking out.
items.explanation: The shortest overhang vibrates fastest, which gives the highest pitch.

items.prompt: A drum is hit. Tap the child who hears the quietest sound.

figure.alt: A drum on the left and three children in a row at different distances. A is the closest, B is in the middle and C is the furthest from the drum.

hints: Sound gets quieter as it spreads out.
Think about how far each child is from the drum.
The quietest sound is heard furthest away.
items.explanation: Sound gets quieter as it travels. Child C is furthest from the drum, so hears the quietest sound.

items.prompt: Kofi measures the sound from a speaker at different distances. The pattern carries on. Complete the table.
head: Distance (m)
Sound level (dB)
hints: Look at how the sound level changes with each metre.
Find the difference between 80 and 72.
The level goes down by 8 dB for every extra metre.
items.explanation: The sound level falls by 8 dB each metre. So 3 m is 64 dB and 5 m is 48 dB.

items.prompt: Use the bar chart. How many decibels louder is the canteen than the library?

figure.alt: Bar chart of sound levels in decibels: library 40, classroom 60, canteen 80, busy road 90.

hints: Read the height of the canteen and library bars.
Subtract the quieter level from the louder level.
The canteen bar is at 80 dB.
items.explanation: 80 - 40 = 40 dB louder.

items.prompt: Which place in the bar chart is exactly 20 dB louder than the classroom?

figure.alt: Bar chart of sound levels in decibels: library 40, classroom 60, canteen 80, busy road 90.

options.text: The library
options.why: The library is quieter than the classroom.

options.text: The busy road
options.why: The road is 30 dB louder than the classroom.

options.text: The classroom
options.why: This is the place we are comparing with.

options.text: The canteen

hints: Find the classroom bar first, at 60 dB.
Add 20 dB to that level.
Which bar is at that height?
items.explanation: 60 + 20 = 80 dB, which is the canteen.

items.prompt: Sound travels through air at about 340 m per second. Leo sees lightning, then hears the thunder 3 seconds later. How far away is the lightning?
hints: Light reaches you almost at once, so the delay is the travel time of the sound.
Distance = speed x time.
Multiply 340 by 3.
items.explanation: 340 m/s x 3 s = 1020 m, so the lightning struck about 1020 m away.

items.prompt: A person puts an ear to a steel railway line and hears a train long before it can be heard through the air. Using the table, why?

head: Material
Speed of sound (m/s)
figure.alt: Table of the speed of sound: air 340 metres per second, water 1500 and steel 5000.

options.text: Sound cannot travel through air at all.
options.why: Sound does travel through air, just more slowly.

options.text: The train makes a different sound in steel.
options.why: The sound is the same, but it travels faster in steel.

options.text: Sound travels faster through a solid such as steel than through air.
Steel is a light source.
options.why: Light does not carry sound.

hints: Compare the speeds in the table.
A higher speed means the sound arrives sooner.
Which row has the biggest number?
items.explanation: Sound travels at 5000 m/s in steel and only 340 m/s in air, so it arrives through the rail sooner.

items.prompt: A bell rings inside a glass jar. A pump slowly removes the air from the jar. What happens to the sound heard outside?

options.text: It gets louder, because the bell is lighter without air.
options.why: Sound needs a material to travel through. Less air here means less sound.

options.text: It gets quieter and quieter, because there is less air to carry the vibrations.
It stays the same, because the bell is still ringing.
options.why: The bell still vibrates, but fewer vibrations reach us.

options.text: The pitch changes to a much higher note.
options.why: Taking away air does not change the pitch.

hints: Sound is carried by vibrating air.
The bell is still moving, but what is missing?
No air at all means no sound reaches your ear.
items.explanation: Sound needs a material to travel through. With less air in the jar, fewer vibrations pass to the glass and out to us.

items.prompt: How high or low a sound is, is called its ___.
hints: It is not the same as loudness.
A flute has a high one and a tuba has a low one.
It starts with the letter p.
items.explanation: Pitch describes how high or low a sound is.

items.prompt: The loudness of a sound is measured in units called ___.
hints: A sound meter shows these units.
The short way to write them is dB.
The word starts with deci.
items.explanation: Loudness is measured in decibels, written dB.

items.prompt: Bigger vibrations make a ___ sound. Faster vibrations make a ___ pitch.
hints: Loudness and pitch are two different things.
Think of a big hit on a drum.
Fast shaking gives a squeak, not a rumble.
items.explanation: Bigger vibrations give a louder sound. Faster vibrations give a higher pitch.

items.prompt: Match each instrument to a way of making its pitch higher.
hints: Higher pitch comes from faster vibrations.
Tight or short things vibrate faster.
The flute has air that vibrates.
items.explanation: Tighter and shorter parts vibrate faster, so they make a higher pitch.

items.prompt: Sort each change into whether it changes the pitch or the loudness.
hints: Pitch is high or low. Loudness is loud or quiet.
Size of vibration changes loudness.
Speed of vibration changes pitch.
items.explanation: Faster vibrations change the pitch. Bigger vibrations or distance change the loudness.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to show how you hear a guitar.
items: A string on the guitar vibrates.
The vibrating string makes the air vibrate.
The vibrations travel through the air to your ear.
Your brain tells you that you heard a sound.
hints: Start with the source.
The air carries the vibrations to your ear.
The brain is the last step.
items.explanation: A vibrating string shakes the air, the vibrations reach the ear and the brain hears a sound.

items.prompt: Choose all the true statements about sound.

options.text: Sound is made by vibrations.
Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases.
Sound travels faster than light.
options.why: Light is far faster than sound. That is why we see lightning first.

options.text: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
A louder sound has a higher pitch.
options.why: Loudness and pitch are different things.

hints: Check each statement on its own.
Sound needs something to travel through.
Remember lightning and thunder.
items.explanation: Sound comes from vibrations and needs a solid, liquid or gas. It cannot travel through empty space.

items.prompt: Two friends make a string telephone with two cups. The string is slack and hangs loosely. They cannot hear each other. Why?

options.text: The vibrations cannot pass well along a slack string, so the sound does not reach the other cup.
A slack string makes no sound at all.
options.why: A tight string carries the sound well. Slack ones do not.

options.text: The cups are too close for the sound to work.
options.why: Closeness is not the problem.

options.text: Sound cannot travel through string.
options.why: Sound travels well along a tight string.

hints: A tight string carries vibrations.
What happens to vibrations along a loose string?
Think of what the friends do to make it work.
items.explanation: Vibrations pass well along a tight string. A slack string does not carry them well, so the sound is lost.

items.prompt: Amara shouts at a cliff and hears her echo 2 seconds later. Sound travels at 340 m per second. How far away is the cliff?
hints: The sound has to go to the cliff and come back.
Find the distance for the whole trip, then halve it.
In 2 seconds sound covers 2 x 340 m. The cliff is half of that.
items.explanation: In 2 s the sound travels 680 m there and back, so the cliff is 340 m away.

items.prompt: Why do workers on a noisy building site wear ear defenders?

options.text: They make the sound louder.
options.why: Defenders are designed to make sound quieter.

options.text: They change the pitch of the sounds.
options.why: They do not change the pitch.

options.text: They stop all vibrations in the ground.
options.why: They only cover the ears.

options.text: They reduce the amount of sound that reaches the ears, which protects hearing.

hints: Very loud sounds can harm the ears.
Defenders are made from soft, thick material.
What does a muffling material do to sound?
items.explanation: Ear defenders absorb sound so less reaches the ear. This protects hearing from very loud noise.

items.prompt: True or false: Sound is made when something vibrates.

options.text: True
False

hints: Touch a speaker.
Do you feel it?
Vibrations make sound.
items.explanation: A drum skin vibrates when it is hit, and this makes sound.

items.prompt: True or false: A louder sound has a higher pitch.

options.text: True
False

hints: What does pitch mean?
Is a loud drum high?
Loud and high differ.
items.explanation: Loudness depends on how big the vibrations are. Pitch depends on how fast they are.

items.prompt: True or false: Faster vibrations make a higher pitch.

options.text: True
False

hints: Think of a short string.
Fast means high.
Speed decides pitch.
items.explanation: More vibrations each second give a higher note.

items.prompt: True or false: Sound can travel through space as there is nothing to stop it.

options.text: True
False

hints: What is space mostly?
What carries a vibration?
No particles, no sound.
items.explanation: Sound needs particles to carry the vibrations, so it cannot travel through the near-empty vacuum of space.
